Alan Bartlett, left, and fellow Leamington High Line CIC director Ian Dunning, middle, along with volunteer Tom Dunn, right, are among the first people to stand on the disused Leamington railway viaduct since it closed

A project to plant five themed gardens on a disused railway viaduct has taken a major step forward, with those behind the scheme getting access to the top of the structure for the first time.

The Leamington High Line Community Interest Company (CIC) has raised enough money to fix a ladder and platform to the first stretch of the viaduct in Bath Place, giving them access to the former track bed.

It comes as the first set of conceptual drawings of what the proposed gardens would look like are published.

Derrick Knight, a director of the CIC said: "We're going to turn this neglected heritage structure into a place the town can enjoy for generations."

The aim is to create five themed gardens connecting the railway station with Leamington's creative quarter and the eastern part of the town.

It is estimated that the scheme, which is being funded through grants and donations, will cost between £10m and £50m and could take up to 10 years to complete.

Five themed gardens running the length of the viaduct are planned, with an estimated cost of up to £50m

The viaduct was built in 1844 and runs from Lower Avenue to the Victoria Business Centre on Neilston Street, a distance of around 500 metres. It originally carried both goods and passengers from the late 1800s up to the 1960s.

It then closed, but the brick-and-masonry arches were not demolished.

Now, 60 years on, campaigners want to turn it into a green travel route over the town.

Woman reveals how she found her 'tribe' years after baby son's death

Arson ravaged venue 'made me who I am - and its name will live on'

The baby who gives the Christmas tractor run a special meaning

The CIC has raised enough money to fix a permanent ladder and platform to the Bath Place end of the viaduct, meaning work to assess the current state of the brickwork and the wildlife that lives in and on the disused line can start.

Alan Bartlett, another director of the project, said: "The first job is to survey carefully for bat roosts and take off some of the self-seeded plants and trees, which are breaking up the brickwork and pushing roots into the arches below, where local businesses trade.

"So clearing them is the first good thing we can do for the structure and for our neighbours."

The aim is to create five gardens running on the viaduct from Lower Avenue through to the Victoria Business Centre on Neilston Street in Leamington Spa

If approved, the plan would see gardens with specific themes created on top of the old track bed.

Faith Garden, including a renovated railway carriage as a cafe and bar

History Garden, telling the story of the viaduct's construction in 1844

Hope Garden, a community allotment with a long table running the length of it

Solar Garden, with pergolas featuring energy-generating solar panels

Sky Garden, the longest of the gardens with seating and a space for community events

Ian Dunning, another of the CIC's directors, said while the first steps in the project have been taken, he estimated most of it could be open to the public in five years time.

"The funding in terms of grants still needs to be unlocked and we're in the process of submitting funding applications."

He thinks the whole scheme would cost between £10m and £50m, although he is confident that the final bill would be lower than than the higher end estimate.

The CIC has appointed the London-based landscape architects Greenwood-Hill to create the initial vision of the planting and scheme.

A spokesperson for the design firm said "the sketches set out some early ideas for how the High Line could become a greener, more accessible and welcoming place for people and wildlife alike.

"It's an exciting community-led vision, and we hope these initial concepts help "people imagine the potential of this unique asset in the heart of Leamington."

Similar projects have been constructed in cities around the world, probably most famously in Manhattan, New York, , external where a stretch of elevated rail line was saved from demolition in the 80s with the first area of parkland opening in 2009.

Seoul in South Korea has a similar park , external , constructed on a stretch of disused highway over the city.

Supporters say they can help promote walking and cycling and sustainably re-use obsolete infrastructure. However, lack of funding can be an obstacle, as demonstrated in in Camden, north London , external , where work on a high line project has stalled because of rising costs.

Dip, swerve, curl, whip. Hours spent mastering the craft of a great free-kick ensure those that ripple the back of the net are particularly satisfying.

This week we are digging into the Premier League's all-time best takers.

The number of goals scored from direct free-kicks has gradually decreased over the past two decades (boo!) with a rising focus on generating higher-quality chances, rather than having a pop from range.

It is perhaps unsurprising then that James Maddison is the only current player in the competition's all-time top 25 free-kick scorers, after James Ward-Prowse returned to Championship side Southampton in the summer.

Dominik Szoboszlai, however, is bucking the trend with five since joining Liverpool from 32 attempts - an impressive conversion rate of 15.6% and almost a third of his total Premier League goals.

He looks on course to become a free-kick great, already only one goal behind Trent Alexander-Arnold and Leighton Baines and just two off the likes of Matt le Tissier, Wayne Rooney and Steven Gerrard.

The majority of top scorers hail from the halcyon era of, essentially, having a dig.

Yaya Toure belongs in another category - he misses out on the top 10 below but could be deemed a 'one-season wonder' in this realm, despite having eight years at Manchester City .

His prolific spell in 2013-14 deserves recognition, scoring four of his seven free-kick attempts that term - a staggering 57.1% conversion rate and by far the Premier League's best since Opta began collecting such data in 2006.

There is also an honourable mention for Louis Saha, the only man in the Premier League era to score a free-kick with each foot - with his left for Manchester United against Southampton in January 2004, and with his right for Everton against Fulham seven years later.

And while we are here, these are the goalkeepers who least liked facing them.

What we are looking for, though, are the real free-kick specialists - those players whose names evoke memories of ball meeting top bins.

For that reason, despite sitting joint-third on the scorers list with 12, Cristiano Ronaldo and Thierry Henry do not make it. They just scored too many goals - and too many great ones - to be renowned specifically for their set-pieces.

Fewer than 7% of Henry's 175 Premier League goals were free-kicks, netting one on average every 21.5 games. Ronaldo, meanwhile, tried his luck 167 times, scoring one roughly every 14 attempts.

The first spot up for grabs could have gone several ways - Maddison, as mentioned, has a decent shout to be included, and likewise Christian Eriksen who netted eight in the Premier League and also laid on 13 free-kick assists.

Frank Lampard has nine goals but also the most attempts on record - and the data only accounts for half his Premier League career.

Ashley Young is the oldest player to score a Premier League free-kick

OK, the case for Ashley Young is in his longevity - he curled in a free-kick during the play-offs to help Watford win promotion in 2006 and was still scoring them almost two decades later.

At 39 years and 148 days old, Young became the oldest player to score a Premier League free-kick in Everton 's win over Wolves in December 2024. His seventh successful free-kick strike in the competition and the final effort of his 50-goal top-flight haul.

Young holds a decent conversion rate, scoring with 10.3% of his 68 top-flight attempts, while also chipping in with nine free-kick assists - only a handful of players have more since 2003-04.

Young's set-piece duties also tend to bookend his career. A trusted specialist at Watford and Aston Villa , he fell behind Ronaldo, Rooney and co at United but still popped up with a memorable long-range free-kick against the Hornets, his boyhood club.

Nolberto Solano netted nine times from free-kicks in the Premier League - although that tally may have been higher had he not shared set-piece duties with Laurent Robert for a chunk of his Newcastle career, while Alan Shearer chipped in too.

In fact, including spells at Aston Villa and West Ham, the Peruvian scored 18% of his top-flight goals with free-kicks.

He had a decent conversion rate. Opta data only goes back to 2003-04, but since then Solano, who also played for Aston Villa and West Ham, netted 10% of all his free-kick attempts on goal.

Solano scored free-kicks throughout his career, including his last goal for League One Hartlepool in 2011

Liverpool legend Steven Gerrard reckons Juan Mata is the best free-kick taker in Premier League history and the only player who outshines current Anfield star Szoboszlai.

I disagree, hence ranking the Spaniard eighth, but Mata can claim to be the most ruthless - he's scored a higher percentage of free-kicks than any player to have had at least 20 attempts since the stat-counting began in 2003-04.

The World Cup winner, who recently retired, netted eight in the English top flight from 49 attempts - an impressive conversion rate of 16.3%.

Morten Gamst Pedersen was plucked from the freezing fjords above the Arctic Circle to score bangers for Blackburn, a left foot as crisp as the icy waters surrounding his former home in Tromso.

The hair-gelled Norwegian netted 34 Premier League goals in eight seasons at Ewood Park, with just shy of 30% of those coming from free-kicks - the fifth-highest proportion in the competition's history.

It puts the winger eighth on the all-time list with 10 goals from 158 free-kick shots - only Lampard and Ronaldo have attempted more since 03-04.

The diminutive Italian announced himself to the Premier League as he meant to go on. In his fourth Chelsea appearance, Gianfranco Zola scored his first goal from a belting long-range free-kick against Everton .

It was the first of 12 in the competition.

What sets Zola apart is all of those came after turning 30, having been a phenomenal set-piece specialist back in Serie A - he remains sixth on the all-time list there with 20, one behind Roberto Baggio and Francesco Totti.

And Zola learned from the best. As a youngster at Napoli, he would seek advice from the legendary Diego Maradona.

"He was always fond of making suggestions and giving advice to young players," Zola said.

"We had a particularly good relationship and I used to stay a bit longer on the training ground with him trying free-kicks and playing small games."

Gianfranco Zola scored 59 goals for Chelsea in the Premier League, with just over 20% of those coming from free-kicks

Something of a rarity, a free-kick expert at full-back - the Drogheda Roberto Carlos, as they used to call him (they didn't).

Ian Harte has, however, previously suggested the Brazilian and David Beckham provided him with dead-ball inspiration, and reckons he has a better conversion rate than that pair.

Harte is joint-eighth on the list of all-time Premier League free-kick top scorers but leaps to fifth here for the specialist nature of his impressive resume. He scored 10 in nine seasons with Leeds , 35.7% of his total Premier League goals.

Fans at Elland Road would also point towards perhaps Harte's finest performance, though, the Champions League quarter-final first leg against Deportivo in 2001 - the Irishman crashed in a free-kick before claiming two assists.

Ian Harte scored 10 free-kicks for Leeds in the Premier League - though his most famous came against Deportivo in Europe

Sebastian Larsson scored 26 Premier League goals, 11 of them directly from free-kicks - the second-highest proportion in the competition's history.

Give away a foul within range and the Swede could be deadly, with an impressive ratio of scoring one from roughly every nine attempts in the top flight.

Indeed, the midfielder is the only player to score at least 30% of his free-kick shots in two separate seasons - 2007-08 with Sunderland and 2011-12 with Birmingham.

"Seb Larsson was a quality player and he had that ability to have a magic moment," fellow ex- Sunderland star Marco Gabbiadini told BBC Radio Newcastle . "When he connected correctly, they were lovely goals."

"I practise free-kicks for about half an hour after each training session. It's not just about mastering technique - it gives you confidence," Larsson told FourFourTwo.

"I visualise the ball going where I want it to go and I don't hold back."

One of Larsson's free-kick goals came against former club Arsenal

Left foot like a trebuchet. Laurent Robert loved nothing more than winding one up from 30-plus yards out, lashing goalwards and hoping the ball hit the back of the net.

And, in fairness, the Frenchman was very good at it. In four seasons with Newcastle , he scored 11 free-kicks, a remarkable 47.8% of his total 23 Premier League goals.

Robert boasts the competition's best free-kick goals-per-minute ratio, netting one every 994 minutes - he did have well over 100 attempts - and is also the only player alongside Beckham to score five in one season.

However, it was one missed free-kick, the story goes, that may have sealed his fate when on loan at Portsmouth. Robert fired wildly into the crowd when trailing 2-1, which was said to have left boss Harry Redknapp fuming. He signed for Benfica a few days later.

Eleven of Laurent Robert's 23 Premier League goals were direct free-kicks

James Ward-Prowse holds good company. According to Opta Analyst, he is one of only six players from Europe's top-five leagues since their data began to score at least 10% of free-kicks, having attempted more than 100. Ronaldinho is among the others.

Ward-Prowse is also second to only Beckham on the all-time Premier League free-kick goalscorers chart, netting 17 of his 141 attempts (12.1%), throughout spells with Southampton, West Ham, Nottingham Forest and Burnley.

A dream pick for Fantasy Premier League managers, there was a time when Ward-Prowse standing over a dead ball felt inevitable - he netted four of his 10 goals in 2021-22 from free-kicks, while another four were penalties.

The midfielder grabbed another three the following season, with his final two proving winners against Everton and Chelsea .

Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola was certainly a big fan, saying: "Southampton have the best free-kick taker I have ever seen, or at least in the world right now."

Overall, almost a third of Ward-Prowse's Premier League goals came from free-kicks, while he leads the way since 2003-04 with 31 dead-ball assists, a third of those from free-kicks.

A trait that transcended football. Beckham's free-kick prowess had Hollywood screenwriters scrambling and kids in classic Predators practising bendy run-ups on muddy weekend mornings.

Beckham has scored more free-kicks in the Premier League era than any other player, not to mention iconic strikes for his country and in the Champions League.

Eighteen of those came in the English top flight, accounting for 29% of his total 62 goals in the competition for Sir Alex Ferguson's Manchester United , and perhaps more impressively 27% of all the free-kicks United have netted in the competition.

Beckham got up and running on his 48th United appearance in October 1996, during a shock 6-3 defeat at Southampton.

That was the first of three set-piece strikes he would score against the Saints, with all of Beckham's free-kick goals coming in different matches, while he netted from a dead ball for the final time with United before his move to Real Madrid in a 2-1 win at Everton in May 2003.

Beckham was deadly when laying on goals for others, too. Of his 80 Premier League assists, more than a quarter came from set-pieces, with 11 of those from free-kicks.

David Beckham scored 18 goals from free-kicks in the Premier League

Ubushakashatsi bushasha bwerekana ko Abongereza, na cane cane imiyabaga n'urwaruka, bagira imibonano mpuzabitsina gake canke ntibayikore na gato ugereranije na bakuru babo. Ariko benshi bararaba amashusho y'ubusambanyi, bakongera bagahanahana ubutumwa buyaga ivy'igitsina.

Ni ubwa mbere ubushakashatsi bwa Natsal, bwiga ubuzima bw'abantu mu vy'imibonano mpuzabitsina, bubajije abantu ku vyo bakorera kuri internet.

Umwe kuri babiri mu bafise imyaka iri hagati ya 16 na 24 yararungitse canke yararonse amafoto ajanye n'igitsina kuri terefone mu mwaka uheze. Umukobwa umwe kuri babiri n'abahungu hafi icenda kuri cumi bavuga ko baravye amashusho y'ubusambanyi (porno).

Ariko umwe kuri batatu muri abo bafise imyaka iri hagati ya 16 na 24 ntarigera arangura amabanga y'abubatse. Mu bushakashatsi bwaheruka gukorwa haciye imyaka 12, yari umwe kuri batanu.

Abantu bakuze batarashikana imyaka 45 na bo basigaye bagira imibonano mpuzabitsina gake. Muri rusangi, bayigira incuro zibiri ku kwezi, ugereranije n'incuro imwe mu ndwi mu 1990.

Abakenyezi barenga umwe kuri batatu, ni ukuvuga ibice 37%, bavuze ko baravye amashusho y'ubusambanyi mu mwaka uheze.

Mu bagabo, ni hafi bane kuri batanu. Ni ukuvuga ibice 81%.

Mu bafise imyaka iri hagati ya 16 na 24, igice c'abakobwa hamwe na 86% vy'abahungu bavuze ko baravye ayo mashusho.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Kuraba ayo mashusho no kwikinisha vyaboneka gake mu batarigera bagira imibonano mpuzabitsina. Abakoze ubwo bushakashatsi bavuga ko ivyo bishobora gusigura ko kwikinisha canke kuraba amashusho y'ubusambanyi kuri internet bitariko birasubirira imibonano mpuzabitsina y'abantu bari kumwe. Ariko ntibarashobora kuvyemeza neza.

Ntibabajije ku buhinga bw'ubwenge bukorano, AI, canke ku migenderanire y'urukundo abantu bashobora kugirana n'amaporogarama ayaga na bo. Ariko babona ko bakwiye kuzobibaza mu bushakashatsi buzokurikira.

Soazig Clifton, umwe mu bakora ubushakashatsi bwa Natsal akaba akorera muri University College London, yavuze ati: "Igihe twegeranya amakuru hagati ya 2022 na 2024, ivyo vyasa n'ibintu vyo mu nkuru z'ivyiyumviro (science-fiction)."

Yongeyeko ati: "Muri kazoza, dushobora kuzokwihweza ingaruka AI igira ku nyifato y'abantu mu vy'imibonano mpuzabitsina no ku migenderanire yabo, nk'igihe baganira n'amaporogarama ya AI nk'aho ari abagenzi babo."

Umwe mu bakoze ubwo bushakashatsi, Pr Wendy Macdowall wo muri London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), avuga ko n'ubwo vyoroshe kwiyumvira ko umwanya abantu bamara baraba muri terefone no mu bindi vyuma ari wo utuma imibonano mpuzabitsina igabanuka, hashobora kuba hari izindi mvo nyinshi, na cane cane mu rwaruka.

Nk'akarorero, urwaruka rwo muri iki gihe runywa inzoga nke ugereranije n'urwo mu myaka iheze. Benshi kandi baracaba muhira ku bavyeyi babo.

Ukwiyongera kw'ingorane zo mu mutwe na kwo gushobora kuba kuri mu vyabiteye, hamwe n'ikiza ca Covid-19 catumye abantu batakibasha gusohoka ngo bahure n'abandi.

Pr Macdowall avuga ko ibiganiro ku bijanye no kwemeranya gukora imibonano mpuzabitsina bishobora gutuma urwaruka rushobora guhitamwo neza nimba ruyikora n'igihe ruyikorera.

Ariko hari abatanezerewe n'ubuzima bwabo mu vy'imibonano mpuzabitsina.

Umukenyezi umwe kuri indwi, ni ukuvuga 14%, yavuze ko agifitiye umubabaro canke ishavu abandi kubera ivyo bamukoreye mu bijanye n'imibonano mpuzabitsina muri kahise.

Igitigiri nk'ico c'abagabo na co cavuze ko giterwa isoni na bimwe mu vyiyumviro canke ivyipfuzo vyabo bijanye n'igitsina.

Ubu bushakashatsi bwa kane bwa Natsal bwerekana ingene ibintu vyagiye birahinduka, ariko ntibushobora gusigura neza imvo zabitumye.

Ubwaheruka, bwakozwe mu 2010, bwerekanye ko kwihutira kugira imibonano mpuzabitsina ari co kintu urwaruka rwinshi rwicuza ku bijanye n'igihe rwabikora ubwa mbere.

Ubu, biboneka ko benshi bahitamwo kurindira igihe kirekire.

Hafi abakobwa babiri kuri batanu, ni ukuvuga ibice 38%, hamwe n'abahungu barenga umwe kuri bane, ni ukuvuga ibice 28%, bavuga ko batarigera bakora imibonano mpuzabitsina. Mu bushakashatsi bwo mu 1990, 2000 no mu 2010, bari hafi umwe kuri batanu.

Mu bakuze bagira imibonano mpuzabitsina, benshi basigaye bayigira gake. Kera bayigira rimwe mu ndwi, ariko ubu ni rimwe mu ndwi zibiri.

Ivyavuye muri ubwo bushakashatsi buheruka vyasohowe mu kinyamakuru c'ubuvuzi The Lancet. Bishingiye ku nyishu z'abantu 6.700 bafise imyaka iri hagati ya 16 na 59, batowe ata kurobanura, mu Bwongereza.

Ibiharuro vyerekana ko Abongereza benshi, na cane cane urwaruka, bagira imibonano mpuzabitsina idakingiye, ishobora gutera imbanyi n'indwara zifatira mu bihimba vy'irondoka.

Ikoreshwa ry'ibinini vyo kwirinda gusama na ryo ryaragabanutse mu bakobwa n'abakenyezi bakiri bato.

N'ubwo biri uko, abakenyezi bavuga ko badashaka kuvyara bariyongereye incuro zibiri mu myaka cumi iheze. Mu bafise imyaka iri hagati ya 16 na 44, bavuye kuri 8% bashika kuri 17%.

Dr Laura Oakley wo muri London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine avuga ati: "Ubushakashatsi n'ingingo za reta bikwiye kwihutira kumenya ibituma ivyo bihinduka: nimba ari ingorane z'ubutunzi, impungenge z'ihindagurika ry'ibihe canke ihinduka ry'ivyo abantu bashira imbere mu buzima. Ivyo birahambaye kuko bigira ingaruka ku gutunganya ibijanye n'amagara y'abantu, ivyo kwitaho abanyagihugu, n'ibijanye n'ingo n'imiryango."

Eric Freeman was also passionate about orchard wassails, vintage farm wagons, local fruit varieties and Morris dancing

A bench has been unveiled in memory of a farmer and conservationist said to be instrumental in saving a rare breed of British cattle from extinction.

The bench in Newent, Gloucestershire, celebrates Eric Freeman, who promoted Gloucester cattle, Cotswold sheep and Gloucestershire Old Spot pigs on his farm in Taynton, and is credited with helping to revive wassailing in the county.

He died in 2023 aged 91, and his friend, cheese maker Charles Martell, remembered: "It would take Eric two hours to get from the library to the post office because he knew everybody and he didn't do short chats."

Freeman's granddaughter, Natasha James, said he would have been "thrilled" by the honour.

The bench overlooks Albion House, where Freeman grew up and where he started a chicken-processing business on his mother's table, which eventually employed 130 people.

In 1972, when Gloucester cattle were near extinction, he and some friends went to an auction where the last herd was up for sale, and decided to save them.

"Lose the breed, and lose all the things they mean to Gloucestershire," he said.

In 2013, King Charles III presented him with a lifetime achievement award for his services to conservation.

He was also a regular on BBC Radio Gloucestershire , with his Freeman of the Farm feature, and a quote from one of his broadcasts features on the plaque: "The town is full of character, it's just my home, and it's a lovely old place. I've got my heart in it."

Around 100 people came for the unveiling of the bench, which was a gift from the Cotswold Cart Horse Society, which Freeman helped to establish in 1996.

Paul Barnett from the Cart Horse Society said Freeman was a "great man" whose legacy continues

"He was a character and knew about the old ways of farming," his granddaughter said.

"He was a fountain of knowledge on the local area; I hope it [the bench] will give people a chance to understand who he was and the place where he lived."

Professional wrestler Bronson Reed has died aged 38, World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) has announced.

The company said the wrestler, whose real name is Jermaine Haley, died on Friday due to medical complications but did not give further details.

Paying tribute, WWE added: "Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague."

They also offered condolences to the Australian's family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, and their daughter.

WWE has been contacted for further comment.

Haley was honoured at the WWE event at Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia on Friday.

The show began with a 10-bell salute for Haley and in his match, Canadian wrestler Kevin Owens wore an armband that read "Bronson" and addressed the crowd.

"I knew for a fact, beyond performing in this ring, he loved his family more than anything so tonight if there is anything to take away from a tragedy like that - it's take care of each other and love each other... Forgive each other," Owens said.

"Bronson, for me, we were lucky to have you and you will be extremely missed."

WWE greats posted tributes online including the retired 16-time world champion Ric Flair, who wrote: "another soldier in our business that left us way too early!"

WWE Hall of Famer Diamond Dallas Page said "I was deeply saddened to read about the passing of Bronson Reed. I couldn't help but think of Eddie. Such a shame. My heart goes out to his friends & family. RIP brother."

WWE wrestler Eddie Guerrero - known as Latino Heat - died of heart failure at age 38 in 2005.

Bronson Reed in action against Dragon Lee during RAW in New York in November.

Australian pro wrestler Brendan Vink, who goes by Duke Hanson, posted "I love you, Jermaine." on X.

According to wrestling media outlets, Haley had recently been recovering from injuries sustained during the WWE Crown Jewel event in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia earlier in November.

He did not have a match during the event but was tossed off the stage and through a set of tables during a brawl.

Haley initially competed around the independent wrestling scene as Jonah Rock and J-Rock before signing with WWE in 2019.

He was released in 2021 before returning a year and continuing with WWE up until his death. In 2024, he won the André the Giant Memorial Battle Royal.

Haley is the second wrestler to die in the last few months after Benjamin Satterley, an English wrestling star passed away at the age of 40 in September.

No cause of death was provided at the time.

Abayobozi ba gisirikare bayobora Guinea-Bissau basubitse amatora yari ateganyijwe mu cyumweru gitaha ku gihe cy'imyaka ibiri.

Perezida w'inzibacyuho, Gen Horta N'Tam, yatangaje ko amatora ya perezida n'ay'abadepite yari ateganyijwe tariki esheshatu Ukuboza (12), atakibaye, akaba yimuriwe ku wa 26 Ugushyingo (11) 2028.

Iri tangazo rije hashize umwaka umwe gusa igisirikare gifashe ubutegetsi, aho cyari cyasezeranyije gusubiza igihugu mu buyobozi bwa gisivili mu gihe kitarenze amezi 12.

Mu itangazo ryasohowe n'ibiro bya perezida, havuzwe ko isuzuma ry'imyiteguro y'amatora ryagaragaje ko hataraboneka ubushobozi buhagije mu bya tekiniki, ibikoresho ndetse n'amafaranga byo gutegura ayo matora nk'uko byari biteganyijwe.

Iryo tangazo rivuga ko gusubika amatora bizatanga igihe gihagije cyo kuyategura neza mu buryo bwizewe, agakorwa binyuze mu mucyo, aho abakandida bose bazahabwa amahirwe angana.

Ibiro bya perezida byanasubiyemo ko byiyemeje gutegura amatora ya mbere y'inzego z'ibanze muri iki gihugu, ariko ntibyatangaje itariki azaberaho.

Gen Horta N'Tam yarahiriye kuyobora igihugu mu nzibacyuho umunsi umwe nyuma y'uko igisirikare gihiritse ku butegetsi Perezida Umaro Sissoco Embaló mu Ugushyingo 2025.

Iryo hirikwa ryabaye hashize iminsi itatu habaye amatora rusange ndetse umunsi umwe mbere y'uko hatangazwa ibyavuye mu matora by'agateganyo.

Embaló n'uwo bari bahanganye cyane, Fernando Dias, bombi bari batangaje ko ari bo batsinze ayo matora.

Embaló, umaze igihe aba mu buhungiro muri Maroc, mu kwezi gushize yabujijwe gusubira muri Guinea-Bissau n'ubwo yari yatangaje ko ashaka kongera kwiyamamaza ku mwanya w'umukuru w'igihugu.

Over a career spanning more than two decades, Gallagher became a familiar face on television, radio and stage

Taoiseach (Irish prime minster) Micheál Martin has led tributes to comedian and broadcaster PJ Gallagher, who has died at the age of 51.

Born in Cork and adopted and raised in Dublin, Gallagher was a familiar presence on television for more than two decades, appearing in numerous programmes, including BBC's The Young Offenders.

He first came to prominence in 2005, co-creating the RTÉ hidden-camera series Naked Camera, which established him as one of Ireland's best-known comedy performers.

As well as his work in stand-up comedy and acting, Gallagher presented television documentaries and was a member of the breakfast show team on Radio Nova.

Posting on social media, Martin described Gallagher as a "gifted comedian, actor and broadcaster" who brought "immense warmth and laughter to so many across Ireland".

Gallagher's agency LR Comedy confirmed his death in a statement on Friday evening, saying his family and friends were "devastated" and asked that they be given privacy and time to come to terms with their loss.

The statement also highlighted how Gallagher spoke with "remarkable candour about his experiences of mental illness", wanting people to "talk about what they were going through without shame".

He published a memoir in 2023 titled Madhouse: The naked truth about my chaotic childhood, losing my mind and finding a place to call home.

Following this he made a documentary called Changing My Mind, which explored mental health issues.

More recently Gallagher headed the RTÉ One series The Random Driving Test, after participating earlier in the year in the second season of Uncharted with Ray Goggins, where he joined actor Liam Cunningham, and Goggins on a motorbike expedition across the Himalayas.

Posting on Bluesky, comedian Dara Ó Briain said Gallagher was "the sweetest soul; and a warm, instinctive, funny-bones performer".

Also paying tribute was Tánaiste (Irish deputy prime minster) Simon Harris who said he was "deeply saddened" by the news, describing Gallagher as a "true treasure of Irish broadcasting and comedy".

On Instagram, podcaster Blindboy Boatclub echoed Ó Briain's comments, describing Gallagher as an "incredibly sweet and kind person".

Carly Rae Jepsen first found fame on Canadian Idol before launching her international career with the single Call Me Maybe

For years, Carly Rae Jepsen's fans have been telling anyone , external who'll listen , external that she wrote the perfect pop song... and they don't mean Call Me Maybe.

No, it's Run Away With Me – three minutes of pure euphoria that captures the moment a crush snowballs into a full-blown love affair.

Released in 2015, it stalled at number 58 in the charts, but it has long been a highlight of Jepsen’s live shows. Then, last week, it made a surprise appearance in Grand Theft Auto VI.

It provides the soundtrack to a pivotal sequence where the game's protagonists get their first taste of the high life - zooming around on jet skis and shooting champagne bottles from the back of a yacht.

"Have I ever done that? I have not!" Jepsen laughs.

"My guilty admission is that I haven't even played the game yet, but I'm excited to try it. I'm gonna become a late-in-life gamer!"

The placement has given the song a new lease of life. Its daily streams rose from 20,000 to 281,000 overnight. On Friday, it re-entered the UK charts at a new peak of 28.

"It's wild," says Jepsen from her home in Los Angeles. "I love a plot twist, and this was exactly that."

In some ways, it’s a vindication for an under-appreciated classic.

"I've always been asked the question, 'When you were in the studio, did you know you had a hit song?'" says Jepsen. "And I always say, 'No. How can anyone know that?'

"However, I will say, with Run Away With Me, out of all the sessions I've ever done in my life, we all felt that thrill that people think you get. We were on our feet, going, 'Oh, this has something special to it'.

"But it never got eyes like it's getting right now, and that makes me believe in that special feeling that we had, when we made it."

The success comes at an interesting juncture in Jepsen’s career.

Over the last decade, Run Away With Me and E•MO•TION, the album it featured on, have become cult classics, helping to establish Jepsen as a favourite among pop connoisseurs.

This year, she rewarded her dedicated fans with a 32-track double album, Day & Night, that spans everything from mellow folk-pop to Abba pastiches and darker, dancefloor-centric experimentation.

It was released as Jepsen, 41, welcomed her first child, Ilya, after falling in love with one of her co-writers, Cole Marsden Greif-Neill, during recording sessions.

She told us more about the music, and her plans for touring with a newborn.

In 2015, E•MO•TION was considered a commercial disappointment – but now it's considered a landmark pop album. How do you look back at it now?

At the time, I remember feeling the pressure of having a song like Call Me Maybe take off. I was nervous about people expecting the same on repeat, knowing that I wasn't capable of delivering that. So E•MO•TION, to me, was a statement of like, 'Here's the type of pop music I love, and here's what I have to offer beyond [Call Me Maybe].'

I'd set my expectations low. I'd taken a break and done Cinderella on Broadway. And when I finally put the album out, I was pretty sure everyone had forgotten what I did. So the fact anyone liked it was a victory.

But did I imagine that it would catapult this new career path for me? I had no insight of that and, looking back at it now, I feel like it was like accidentally strategic for my [type of] success, which is finding people who want something true and authentic and artful, versus Call Me Maybe 2.0.

And that freedom led you to a place where you can release a double album.

Oh, absolutely! There are songs on this album that would normally be locked away in folders on my hard drive. On many songs, I felt like, 'Is this too weird?' But the mission statement with Day & Night was to stop asking that question.

Jepsen is planning her first tour as a mum - and says she's been getting tips from other female artists like Sarah McLachlan

I notice you singing in new ways. You're almost whispering on After All, then That's Just Me is a classic torch song.

Yes, it was actually really fun. My uncle and aunt were visiting from Canada, and they were like, 'Can we hear some demos?' And I played them some stuff, and they were like, 'I would not know this was you'.

I felt like that was such a feat in its own right, to put out something fresh after so many years in the business.

How did you decide what was a 'Day' song and what was a 'Night' one?

The Day songs are more organic. Folky, psychedelic pop is where I would land with it. At night, we go a little bit more synth-based, like a dance party in my house.

The first track you wrote was a 'Night' song: No Labels, I Love You

Yes, with my partner, Cole, who's now my husband.

Was that session the first time you met?

It was, yeah, in the parking lot at Henson Studios. We were friends for a whole year before we started dating, but there was definitely some chemistry and excitement there.

After that session, I was trying to save his contact details, and because the song we'd written was No Labels, I Love You, I wrote, ' Cole I Love You ' in my phone.

Turns out the joke's on me! I kept the contact in my phone that way forever.

The singer made her Glastonbury festival debut in 2023, with a well-received performance on The Other Stage

One of my favourite songs is Blue Skies, and the opening lyric is, 'I said I love you first'. Is that autobiographical?

No, the funny thing is, we had a trip to Japan, and I had this big idea that I was going to tell him I loved him on top of the Tokyo Tower. I felt like doing something cinematic and ridiculous... but he beat me to it. He told me three days before when we were in Hakone, in the spa!

So if the relationship was developing as the album was being written, has it become a document of that romance?

I mean, there's a heck of a lot of songs that are dedicated to Cole, but there's other moments where I'm literally writing with him, and we're talking about something from my past, and those songs are threaded in there, too.

The singer met her husband, Cole, on the first day of recording her eighth album, Day & Night.

Well, congratulations to you both. And congratulations on becoming parents, too! Your son's name is Ilya, right?

Yes, Ilya. Weirdly, he is getting cuter every day, which is saying something because he started off cute.

Every day, I'm seeing a new facial expression, like a new little nose scrunch or something. It's wild.

Have you spoken to any other musicians for advice on touring with a toddler?

I can get so much advice from my mom and my girlfriends about raising kids, but none of them have been on tour – so I spoke to Sarah McLachlan, who gave me loads of tips. But what's really in my corner is the amount of people, and women who have kids specifically, on this tour with me.

So the way we've planned for time off, and even the buses we're picking are very suited for children. I'm not in it alone.

How do you make a tour bus suitable for children?

You need to have a place for the pack'n'play [travel cot]. You have to change how the bathroom is. But we're also looking at how we handle the long drives.

I'm quite cockily talking about it with confidence before I've done a run. Catch me on the flip side and I might be like, 'Don't ever do it!'

Jepsen is also working on a musical production of the hit romcom 10 Things I Hate About You, alongside writer and actress Lena Dunham and playwright Jessica Huang

With 32 new songs, how will you plan the setlist?

I know, right? We'll be like Bruce Springsteen, playing late into the night.

I mean, we'll see how long my voice lasts...

On top of everything else, you're also working on the musical version of 10 Things I Hate About You. How's that going?

This is year six of working on that show, isn't that crazy?

They take a hot minute, but now we've had workshops in New York with actors and choreography and staging.

What we're trying to do is honour how hilarious the story is. Because when I go to a show I want to cry, I want to laugh, and I want to leave 10 pounds lighter, feeling great about the world.

If it can have all those things, it'll be a success in my eyes.

Abakozi babiri b'ikigo citaho amagara y'abantu gikukira Ishirahamwe ry'Abaganga Batagira Imbibe 'Médecins Sans Frontières' (MSF) biciwe mu gitero Israel yagavye kuri Gaza, nk'uko iryo shirahamwe ribivuga.

MSF yavuze ko ico gitero catumberejwe neza na neza kuri rimwe mu mavuriro yayo, kandi ko igisirikare ca Israel cari gisanzwe kizi aho riherereye.

Mw'itangazo, igisirikare ca Israel (IDF) cavuze ko abo bantu babiri bari abarwanyi ba Hamas, "bakora akazi ko gucungera umutekano kw'ivuriro rya MSF". IDF yongeyeko ko ico gitero "kitari kigamije ibitaro" kandi ko kitigeze conona ibikoresho canke inyubakwa zikoreshwa mu buvuzi.

Umukuru w'Ishirahamwe Mpuzamakungu ry'Amagara y'Abantu (OMS/WHO) yavuze ko ibitero bigabwa ku bitaro n'amavuriro canke ku bakozi bo kwa Muganga muri Gaza "bibabaje" kandi "bidakwiye kwihanganirwa".

Mu butumwa yashize kuri X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus yanditse ati: "Abashira ubuzima bwabo mu kaga kugira ngo bakize abandi bakwiye gukingirwa, aho guterwa."

Mw'itangazo ryayo, MSF nayo yavuze ko abo bakozi babiri bishwe bari abacungera umutekano. Yongeyeko ko ico gitero catumye igitigiri c'abakozi bayo biciwe muri Gaza kigera kuri 17.

Iryo shirahamwe ryavuze ko "ryababaye cane" ryongera "riratuntura", ryongerako riti: "Inyubakwa zacu zari zifise ibimenyetso bigaragara neza vya MSF, kandi aho ziherereye twari twarahamenyesheje igisirikare ca Israel. Cari kihazi."

Mu butumwa bwaco kuri X, igisirikare ca Israel cavuze ko abo bagabo babiri cise Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira na Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, bari "ivyihebe biri mw'ishami rya gisirikare rya Hamas".

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Igisirikare ca Israel congeyeko ko ivyo ari akandi karorero kerekana ukuntu Hamas "yinyegeza mu mashirahamwe mpuzamakungu".

Cashimangiye ko imbere y'ico gitero, "hafashwe ingingo zibereye zo kwiyubara kugira ngo hagabanuke ingaruka ku basivire". Congeyeko ko abo bagabo bari "bamaze gutegura imigambi yo kugaba ibitero ku basivire n'abasirikare ba Israel".

Intureka zarabandanije muri Gaza kuva Israel na Hamas bemeye guhagarika intambara, biciye mu mugambi w'amahoro wari uhagarariwe na Reta Zunze Ubumwe za Amerika, muri Gitugutu (10) umwaka uheze. Ibikorwa vy'ubutabazi na vyo biracari mu bihe bibi cane. Imvura nyinshi yaguye mu ntango z'uku kwezi yateye imyuzure, yongera yonona amahema n'utuzu tw'impunzi ibihumbi n'ibihumbi.

ONU n'abafatanyabikorwa bayo basavye Israel, igenzura aho abantu binjirira n'aho basohokera muri Gaza, kwemerera kwinjiza ibindi bikoresho vyofasha Abanyapalestina kwitegurira igihe c'imbeho. Ivyo birimwo amahema, ibikoresho vyo kwiyunguruza, amapompo y'amazi, hamwe n'incanco n'imiti.

Intambara yo muri Gaza yatanguye inyuma y'igitero cagabwe na Hamas ku bumanuko bwa Israel ku wa 7 Gitugutu 2023. Ico gihe abantu bababa 1.200 barishwe, abandi 251 na bo bagirwa imbohe na Hamas.

Kuva ico gihe, abantu barenga 74.770 baramaze kwicwa mu bitero vya Israel muri Gaza, nk'uko ubushikiranganji bw'amagara y'abantu bubivuga.

Médecins Sans Frontières says the number of its staff who have been killed in Gaza has risen to 17

Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.

MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.

In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.

The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".

In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."

In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.

The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "​Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."

In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".

The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".

It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".

Witnesses told the BBC the two men were sitting at the clinic entrance when an Israeli drone descended and fired a missile.

Video footage from the scene of the strike showed a small crater beside a plastic chair, with bloodstains and limited damage in a courtyard behind the medical clinic.

Hundreds of Palestinians have since attended the funeral of the MSF workers, carrying the two bodies, wrapped in white plastic bags and placed on stretchers, on their shoulders as they made their way through the streets of the city.

Mohammed Imad, a close friend of Abu Hasira, one of the men killed, said he had seen him just hours before the attack.

"He was a peaceful, kind-hearted man. His only concern was looking after his wife, his two children and his mother," he told the BBC.

He said Abu Hasira had no affiliation with any armed group and had worked at the clinic for a long time.

The two workers' deaths follow an increase in Israeli strikes across Gaza over the past week.

Gaza's civil defence spokesman said eight Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks across the Strip during the day, including the two MSF workers.

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.

At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.

The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,770 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Brian Barry-Murphy will lean on the likes of Ollie Tanner, who scored in Cardiff's 2-0 win over Swansea in 2023, in his first south Wales derby

It can be difficult to change the narrative in sport. Take Cardiff City and their rivalry with Swansea City.

For years, a certain idea had taken hold, that the Swans - their players, staff, the club as a whole - had a better understanding of what the south Wales derby meant, and that innate grasp of its significance had given them the upper hand.

Results have supported the theory. Since a nine-year period at the start of this century where there were no derbies, Swansea have won 11 out of 21 and become the first team in the fixture's century-long history to do the double – that is, to win both league meetings in one season – before repeating the feat the following campaign.

Once a pattern is set in motion, it can take some stopping but, by winning their past two home derbies, Cardiff felt the tide might have been turning.

Granted, the most recent of those triumphs still ended with their relegation to League One two seasons ago, but there was at least a feeling that the hoodoo had been lifted.

Nearly two years have passed since the last south Wales derby. In that time, Cardiff have made an instant return to the Championship under head coach Brian Barry-Murphy, who has introduced a refreshingly bold and attacking style of play, built around a core of young local players.

They are still behind their neighbours, though.

Cardiff travel to Swansea on Sunday 17th in the table, nine places and nine points adrift of their opponents.

The Bluebirds have caught the eye with their performances this season but, for all their ambition and stylish dominance of possession, the defensive risks that come attached mean that they are still searching for a first away win of the campaign.

You have to go back nine derbies for the last time Cardiff won in Swansea, and a decade further back again for the last time they triumphed there with fans present.

What an opportunity this weekend's reunion presents, then, to shift another narrative.

"You have to accept it's a different game," says Barry-Murphy, preparing for his first south Wales derby.

"It's not a normal game, and I think if you try to make out as if it's just another game, you're preparing for something that's not going to happen.

"This is a totally different fixture for our players because the atmosphere is going to be totally different.

"We have to show that we have the characteristics and personality to perform the way we want to perform in that heat of battle and show who we want to be as a team.

"We're a very aggressive team and have a lot of daring players who play on the front foot. Our intention on Sunday, despite whatever the opposition do, is to show that version of ourselves."

Cardiff players will have 'edge' against Swansea

There will be a marked difference between this freewheeling Cardiff side and the previous, cagier iterations to make the short trip down the M4 to face Swansea, who have built their identity around a progressive football philosophy over the past 20 years.

If that represents a hint of convergence between the two rivals on the pitch, then one area where the clubs have certainly flipped the script is managerial upheaval.

For more than a decade, this fixture had symbolised the dysfunctional running of Cardiff; between 2011 and 2023, none of their managers had lasted long enough to oversee two derbies in one season.

Erol Bulut bucked that trend, only to get sacked less than a month after he was sent off during a 1-1 draw at the Swansea.com Stadium.

Now, Cardiff finally have the stability they have craved – and it is Swansea who have to contend with changes in the dugout.

The Swans are looking for a third permanent head coach since the Bluebirds appointed Barry-Murphy in the summer of 2025.

It is a far cry from the situation four years ago.

After the third of four successive wins over Cardiff, Swansea's head coach at the time, Russell Martin, said their greater stability was one of the reasons for their success against rivals who had a different man at the helm for each of those four defeats.

Former captain Ashley Williams is in charge of the Swans temporarily - assisted by fellow club greats Joe Allen, Leon Britton and Kristian O'Leary - while they look for a full-time successor to Vitor Matos.

Given the abrupt nature of Matos' departure and the ongoing search for his replacement, could this be a good time to face Swansea?

"Maybe, maybe not," says Cardiff vice-captain Rubin Colwill, who is almost certain to wear the armband on Sunday.

"I think the focus for us is us. We've worked really hard, we're really nailed on in what we're doing, and I think that's the most important thing, regardless of any situation that they're experiencing at the moment."

Colwill embodies Cardiff's new ethos: the creative heartbeat of the team and a young, maturing Welsh talent flourishing with the greater responsibility he has been given by Barry-Murphy.

Growing up as a Bluebirds fan in Neath, closer to Swansea than the Welsh capital, the 24-year-old also has a strong sense of what this rivalry means on both sides of the divide.

Colwill featured from the bench in Cardiff's thumping 3-0 win when the teams last met in January 2025, while he was an unused substitute when his side won in Swansea five years ago.

He has yet to start a south Wales derby but, as a leader of this new-look Cardiff, Colwill is bound to put that right on Sunday.

"We're all really comfortable with this style of play," he says.

"It's just fine-tuning that last little bit and we'll turn those dominant performances into big victories. Hopefully that will start on Sunday."

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has counter-sued Apple, alleging that the iPhone maker stole trade secrets through a former employee.

In a federal lawsuit filed in July, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company and two of its employees who previously worked for Apple, claiming it had engaged in a "pattern of theft" of proprietary information.

A countersuit, filed in California on Friday, alleged that Apple gained confidential information through the hiring of a former OpenAI employee and accuses it of discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.

Apple denied the counterclaims, describing them as "a transparent attempt to distract from the substance" of its own case.

OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal devices, which it claims in the countersuit could threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf".

The filing alleged Apple had gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who had worked at OpenAI for six months.

OpenAI accused the employee, who it said gained access to information on a new device and the company's roadmap for future physical products, of sending "dozens of OpenAI documents" to his personal phone numbers. It also said he presented OpenAI's plans to senior Apple staff "at Apple's request".

OpenAI said: "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place."

The counterclaim also alleged Apple encourages employees to mix work files with their personal iCloud (Apple's cloud storage service) accounts so it could later accuse those who leave to work for competitors of theft.

A spokesperson for Apple said: "This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products - not about inadvertent retention of Apple information."

In its own lawsuit, the tech giant alleged that at least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI took part in a "pattern of theft" by emailing themselves internal Apple information.

Apple also accused the AI firm of undertaking a "strategy to extract Apple's confidential information".

A spokesperson for OpenAI previously denied the claims, telling the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets."

Along with OpenAI, and two former Apple employees, Apple is also suing io Products, the design startup founded by Sir Jony Ive, a long-time Apple executive who designed the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad.

OpenAI acquired the company last year in a $6.5bn (£4.7bn) deal.

This graphic summarises Rwanda’s Local Government

The month-long local government electoral season has come to an end, with district leadership teams across Rwanda now fully constituted, except in the three City of Kigali districts of Nyarugenge, Kicukiro and Gasabo, which operate under a different administrative arrangement.

The hard part begins now: delivering on the country’s development agenda over the next five years.

The new leadership teams, elected between November 17 and 24, 2026, bring a mix of new faces and returning leaders. They also reveal an interesting picture of women’s representation in local government, with women securing eight of the 27 mayoral positions and 31 of the 81 positions across district Executive Committees.

The eight female Mayors represent 29.6% of the total, slightly below the constitutional requirement of at least 30% women’s representation in decision-making organs. However, when the two Deputy Mayor positions in each district are included, women’s overall representation rises to 38.3%.

Men hold the remaining 50 positions in the 27 district Executive Committees, representing 61.7%.

Eighteen of Rwanda’s 27 districts have elected new Mayors, while nine outgoing leaders secured another five-year term.

The eight districts under women’s leadership are Musanze, Ngoma, Nyabihu, Gakenke, Kamonyi, Rwamagana, Rulindo and Ruhango.

Six women are taking up the positions for the first time, while Vestine Mukandayisenga of Gakenke and Nathalie Niyonagira of Ngoma retained their positions.

The newly elected female Mayors are Marie-Grâce Berwa in Musanze, Jacqueline Uwingabire in Nyabihu, Patricia Murekatete in Kamonyi, Sandra Musabwasoni in Rwamagana, Chantal Uwamahoro in Rulindo and Virginie Mukasonga in Ruhango.

The nine returning Mayors are Gerald Muzungu of Karongi, Narcisse Mupenzi of Nyamasheke, Phanuel Sindayiheba of Rusizi, Fred Hategekimana of Kayonza, Prosper Mulindwa of Rubavu, Bruno Rangira of Kirehe and Henry Kakooza of Nyagatare, alongside the two women leading Gakenke and Ngoma.

The remaining districts have new leaders, including Vedaste Nshimiyimana in Huye, Jean-Léonard Sekanyange in Gatsibo, Ildephonse Niyibizi in Burera and Pierre Célestin Bimenyimana in Nyanza.

Some of the new Mayors are not newcomers to local administration. Thaddée Habimana, elected in Nyamagabe, previously served as the district’s Deputy Mayor in charge of Economic Development.

While women have secured a substantial share of district leadership positions, their representation differs sharply between the two Deputy Mayor portfolios.

Of the 27 Deputy Mayors responsible for Social Affairs, women occupy 18 positions, representing 66.7%. Men hold the remaining nine.

The situation is almost the opposite in economic affairs, where women secured only five of the 27 positions, equivalent to 18.5%.

The five districts with women serving as Deputy Mayors in charge of Economic Development are Burera, Gicumbi, Nyamagabe, Nyaruguru and Ngororero. Men occupy the positions in the other 22 districts.

The imbalance is particularly evident in the Eastern Province, where all seven Deputy Mayors responsible for Social Affairs are women, but none of the seven economic affairs positions went to a woman.

In the Northern Province, no woman was elected Deputy Mayor in charge of Social Affairs, while two women secured positions overseeing economic affairs.

Four districts – Ngoma, Rwamagana, Kamonyi and Ruhango – have women occupying two of the three Executive Committee positions: District Mayor and Deputy Mayor in charge of Social Affairs. Men hold the economic affairs portfolios in all four districts.

A breakdown of all three Executive Committee positions by province shows that the Eastern Province has the highest proportion of women, with nine occupying 21 positions, representing 42.9%.

The Southern Province follows with 10 women among 24 positions, equivalent to 41.7%.

The Northern and Western provinces have the same proportion of women, at 33.3%. The Northern Province has five women among 15 Executive Committee members, while the Western Province has seven among 21.

However, the two provinces differ considerably in the number of districts led by women. Women head three of the Northern Province’s five districts, compared with only one of the Western Province’s seven districts.

Unlike elections in which residents directly vote for their district leaders, Mayors and their two deputies are selected by district councils through an indirect, secret-ballot process.

The councils were constituted through elections held on November 17 for women representatives and November 21 for general councillors, alongside representatives of special-interest groups.

Each District Executive Committee comprises three members: the Mayor, the Deputy Mayor in charge of Economic Development and the Deputy Mayor responsible for Social Affairs.

The three City of Kigali districts – Gasabo, Kicukiro and Nyarugenge – were not included in the district council elections because they do not have independent District Councils and operate under a different administrative arrangement.

The newly elected Mayors and their Executive Committees will serve from 2026 to 2031, overseeing district development programmes, budgets and service delivery.

With most districts getting new leadership, the next five years will test the ability of the incoming administrations to turn their mandates into measurable improvements in residents’ lives.

For women, the election results mark progress in local government representation. But their limited presence in economic development positions shows that representation alone does not guarantee an equal share of leadership responsibilities.

Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.

The Argentinian government had called for the venture to be blocked as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected Argentina's claim.

In a decision on Saturday, the court's president said there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal is unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.

In a vote 18 to 3, judges from the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea rejected Argentina's challenge.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.

But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.

In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim in 1982, sparking a 74-day war over the territory as a British military task force ejected them.

The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.

Rwanda’s list of five-star hotels and luxury hospitality establishments has grown to 12 following the addition of two Kigali hotels in the latest national hotel classification exercise.

The Rwanda Development Board (RDB) awarded five-star classification to The Pinnacle Boutique Hotel and Mövenpick Hotel Kigali during the Rwanda Tourism Forum and Awards 2026, held on November 27 at Kigali Serena Hotel.

The recognition brings the number of establishments on Rwanda’s five-star list to 12, adding to a collection of high-end hotels, resorts and safari lodges that serve the country’s growing tourism market.

The two hotels were among five establishments that received new classifications following the 2026 hotel grading exercise, conducted under the East African Community (EAC) Hotel Classification Criteria.

A five-star hotel represents the highest level of international accommodation, facilities and customer service in a country’s classification system.

It is expected to offer exceptional comfort, spacious and well-equipped rooms, quality restaurants, recreational facilities, professional multilingual staff, 24-hour reception, personalised guest services, strong security and high standards of hygiene. Beyond physical facilities, five-star status requires consistently excellent service, attention to detail and an outstanding guest experience.

Three other establishments attained four-star status: Kigali Delights Hotels and Apartments, Kigali Paramount Hotel and Touch Africa Residence.

The exercise also saw six establishments attain three-star classification, one receive two stars and two others receive one star.

With the latest exercise, the total number of hospitality establishments graded by RDB has reached 266.

The classification programme is part of efforts to improve hospitality standards, encourage investment in quality infrastructure and strengthen Rwanda’s competitiveness as a tourism destination.

Irène Murerwa, RDB Chief Tourism Officer, said the latest recognition reflected progress in raising standards across the hospitality industry.

“Today’s recognition represents a step in the right direction as we continue to raise hospitality standards across Rwanda. As we work towards our tourism revenue targets, we encourage businesses to continue investing in their facilities, people and systems,” she said.

She added that providing visitors with consistent, high-quality services requires collective responsibility across the tourism industry.

The hotel classification awards were presented during the Rwanda Tourism Forum and Awards 2026, organised by RDB in collaboration with the Rwanda Chamber of Tourism.

The forum, held under the theme “Smart Tourism for High-Value Growth: Leveraging Digital Innovation, AI and Sustainability”, brought together tourism and hospitality industry players to discuss ways of improving service delivery, adopting digital solutions and developing a competitive workforce.

The discussions come as Rwanda pursues a target of generating $1.1 billion in annual tourism revenue by 2029.

Two panel discussions examined the role of artificial intelligence and digital technology in improving business visibility, customer engagement, bookings, payments and visitor experiences.

Another focused on customer care, professional standards, service excellence and the skills needed to prepare the tourism workforce for the future.

The event also featured the launch of a Centralised Online Membership Management System by the Rwanda Chamber of Tourism, developed in collaboration with TradeMark Africa. The platform is intended to improve membership management and service delivery.

Aimable Rutagarama, Chairman of the Rwanda Chamber of Tourism, said the annual forum and awards could eventually develop into a fully fledged Rwanda Tourism Week.

He said the expanded platform would create opportunities for tourism businesses to showcase their products, establish commercial partnerships, attract investment and access international markets.

The forum concluded with the Rwanda Tourism Awards 2026, which recognised businesses and professionals for contributions to service excellence, innovation, sustainability and tourism development.

The Pinnacle Boutique Hotel was named Accommodation Establishment of the Year, adding to its recognition through the five-star classification.

Other winners included Rickshaw Travels Rwanda Ltd, named Tour Operator of the Year; Kultura Flavours of Asia, Restaurant of the Year; and Pili Pili, Bar of the Year.

Lanoche Kigali won Nightclub of the Year, while C A Bashana General Enterprises Ltd received the Coffee Shop of the Year award.

Cole Palmer joined Chelsea from Man City for £42.5m in 2023

Cole Palmer left the City Ground without having a shot or a touch in the opposition box as Chelsea lost 3-2 at Nottingham Forest on Friday night.

The 24-year-old forward started the season by registering six goal involvements in his first six league games (two goals and four assists), with his penalty against Manchester United now his only goal contribution in the past six matches.

Last weekend, after his side were booed off following the 4-1 defeat by Leeds United , Palmer appeared reluctant to take part in the customary post-match acknowledgement of the supporters.

On his way off the pitch, he appeared to ignore the club's player support and development officer Willie Isa, a former Wigan Warriors rugby league player, whose role includes helping to ensure that acknowledgement takes place regardless of the result.

Palmer was then seen in a heated exchange with injured striker Joao Pedro as he headed down the tunnel.

His visible frustration comes during a difficult period for Chelsea under new manager Xabi Alonso.

Chelsea have lost their past three games and conceded 23 goals, their highest total after 12 matches since the 2015-16 season, with Alonso facing criticism for the leaky defence and constant line-up changes .

One positive had been the attack, with Chelsea scoring 18 times in six matches, largely because of the link-up play between Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro.

Club-record signing Rogers, who cost £117m in the summer, has also become less effective, while Pedro remains sidelined by a groin injury.

But some observers argue Palmer needs to step up to help lift his team out of this difficult period.

It is nearly two years since he produced the form of his life, breaking Chelsea 's record with 39 goal involvements (26 goals and 13 assists) in the 2024 calendar year.

Now many are asking whether he can return to that level.

There are no concerns about Palmer's attitude or behaviour internally at Chelsea .

Senior sources inside the club say he has been ultra-focused behind the scenes, doing extra sessions and he is described as a "leader" by Alonso.

Both Palmer and Chelsea seem fully committed to each other.

In mid-April, deep into a dismal campaign in which Chelsea finished 10th having had three different managers, rumours were rife he was pining for a return to Manchester, with United - a club he still supports - linked.

When speaking to the Guardian, he added: "All my family are there, but I don't miss it. Maybe I'll miss it if I don't go for three months or something. But then when I get home I think there's nothing there for me anyway. I've got no plans to move from Chelsea ."

A move to United was never seriously explored by any of those involved and Palmer re-established his commitment to Chelsea by signing a lucrative deal until 2034.

It made him among the club's highest-paid players and followed similar deals for Reece James, Moises Caicedo and Joao Pedro.

Palmer's mother, father and girlfriend were all present in the directors' box against Bournemouth after he signed the new deal.

Like the others who have recently renewed, Palmer has been reassured by the sporting leadership team that Chelsea are ambitious, out to win trophies and have learned from past mistakes, hiring a high-calibre manager in Alonso and signing three over-30 players for the first time in four years to add experience to their squad.

That said, Palmer has not hit the heights of his first 18 months under former manager Mauricio Pochettino, now in charge of Manchester United , and then early into Enzo Maresca's reign.

Having been nicknamed "Cold" Palmer after his goal celebration, where he shrugs his shoulders and pretends to be cold, his decline began in early 2025.

A persistent groin problem affected his form as the goals and assists began to dry up. Even so, Palmer produced man-of-the-match displays in the Conference League and Club World Cup finals to maintain his reputation as a big-game player.

He did not fully overcome the injury heading into the following season and his return of 10 goals and one assist in 25 matches represented a significant drop in output.

In a candid pre-season interview , Palmer explained: "The first few months, with me being injured, I just wanted to go out and play, which I probably shouldn't have done.

"Obviously I couldn't play how I wanted to play. It was a bad season personally with injuries but I feel good now."

He added the impact on how he wanted to play affected his ability to move on the pitch and strike the ball with power.

Palmer has also found the situation with England unhelpful.

Over the summer, he was said by multiple sources close to him and inside Chelsea to have been bitterly disappointed to have missed out on the World Cup squad.

It has been further impacted by criticism from manager Thomas Tuchel, who said he "misses too many opportunities" to play for the Three Lions.

Sources at Stamford Bridge also reiterated Alonso's assertion that Palmer was unavailable throughout the extended England camp because of a muscle injury.

It was highlighted by the fact he did not take part in a behind-closed-doors friendly against Portsmouth towards the end of the break.

Palmer was then not selected for the following camp in November, but multiple sources say he remains fully committed to regaining his place in the national team.

Team-mate Rogers told BBC Sport it was "a lie" that Palmer does not want to play for England , while another of his best friends in football, Tosin Adarabioyo, called it "false, false, false".

Former Manchester City and Chelsea defender Tosin, now at Tottenham , is known to have called him a "little superstar", and Palmer has found fame difficult to cope with at times.

The Wythenshawe-born forward is mobbed whenever he leaves Stamford Bridge, while he has posted pictures going out in a balaclava to try to live as normal a life as possible.

Chelsea fan Savage Dan thinks Cole Palmer's inconsistency is 'an issue'

Lastly, there is the question of whether the Chelsea project itself could be impacting him.

The club's use of ultra-long contracts has attracted criticism from some commentators and external sources, who have questioned whether such deals can affect motivation once a player's future is secured.

Critics also argue such contracts may reduce a player's leverage if they later seek a move away.

There is little evidence to support that argument in individual cases, such as Palmer's, but contracts of that length remain rare elsewhere in English football.

Chelsea maintain their deals are heavily incentivised, with significant elements linked to individual and collective performance.

Ultimately, Palmer is one of many Chelsea players struggling, with teams adapting to deal with his threat and he has lost Joao Pedro, with whom he had a fantastic connection .

However, he has the influence to positively affect his team-mates as one of the poster boys for the club and carries the weight of helping his team arrest their downturn.

It now looks as though Palmer's success or failure is completely intertwined with Chelsea 's fortunes, given he will likely remain at the club for a long time to come.

The Blues have shown belief in coaxing Palmer's extraordinary performances of 2024 back out of him and, should that be realised, it would go a long way towards reviving Alonso's side.

Jake Bugg's latest album is called Alamo

"The difficult part was deciding whether to release it or not."

Jake Bugg says writing his latest album was an opportunity to explore loss, regrets and the lessons he has learned along the way.

After enjoying success with his self-titled debut album in 2012, the Nottingham singer says he has since struggled to maintain relationships and ended up feeling isolated.

Despite such a personal record potentially leaving him "very vulnerable", he decided "if somebody can take a slight bit of comfort in this record then the music's bigger than myself".

Best known for the single Lightning Bolt, Bugg released six albums between 2012 and 2024.

But his latest, Alamo, reflects a difficult period in his life.

Bugg first came to prominence through the BBC Introducing strand

"I don't want to go into too many specifics, but it's a combination of things I struggled with," he told the BBC.

"I'd lost a lot of people close to me in a very short space of time, then came a really tough time with relationships - and trying to keep something like that together, while everything else was going on was very difficult. In the end, it was impossible.

"And then you also have the frustrations with the work side of things as well, and things from childhood that I'm only starting to face.

"All of these things led ultimately to isolation.

"Being on your own and trying to make sense of it all and trying, in some ways, to self-medicate.

"So that's the theme of the record: Life builds up and gets the best of us all, sometimes."

Bugg, who grew up on a council estate in the Clifton area of Nottingham, has maintained his links with the city .

But the turmoil of the years since has informed much of this latest record.

He said: "I said a lot of things when I was younger that were just ridiculous, to be honest. When I started, I didn't really know what I was doing really.

"I'd be quite honest about most things, but not necessarily in a positive or a good way. And yeah, I wish I could kind of go back and word things a little bit better."

Bugg continued: "Everywhere I Go is the last song on the record, and it's a bit of a tough listen for me if I'm honest, because it gives me flashbacks to some of these points in my life that that I'm singing about.

"That song is about carrying all of that around with you and not really realising it and the fact you can't ever escape it.

"I've been a bit worried to lean into the darker side, a little bit worried about what people may think. But this record for me allowed me to really go down those rabbit holes."

While struggling with elements of his life, this surprisingly resulted in a more straightforward creative process.

"If anything, it was quite easy and natural because it was so honest," he said.

"The difficult part was deciding whether to release it or not - because it's quite personal and you're leaving yourself very vulnerable.

"But I came to the decision to release the record because I know how much of an impact other people's records had on me growing up.

"I thought, if somebody can take a slight bit of comfort in this record then the music's bigger than myself."
